notes.text: Your pawn takes a share of the centre and stops White from playing e4 freely.
This is the Queen's Gambit: White offers the c-pawn, but could win it back, so you can take or decline.
notes.original:
This is the beginning of the Queen's Gambit! The Queen's Gambit is not really regarded as a "gambit" because after 2. dxc4 white could just win the pawn back with 3. Qa4+, but white usually plays something else.
Black has two options:
1. Accept the gambit by taking c4
2. Decline it by playing something else
I have divided this study into four sections.
- Queen's Gambit Accepted
- Queen's Gambit Declined
- Slav/Semi-Slav Defense
- Move 2 sidelines
There are many defenses for black, but hopefully I have covered most of them. I've also added plenty of traps :)
Note: my lines will not always be the absolute top engine move, they are rather based on which one is more comfortable to play as a human and have a decent winrate.
Go to the next chapter! :)

notes.text: A flexible move: it usually leads to a Queen's Gambit, but can also become a Colle System.
notes.original: A flexible developing move. While this move usually leads to a Queen's Gambit, it is also used to go into a Colle System—a solid line that prepares e2-e4 earlier and can be more aggressive than the usual lines.

notes.text: The knight blocks White's c-pawn, so it can't challenge d5; the line is sound but slow and strategic.
notes.original:
The Chigorin Variation (Named after Mikhail Chigorin) is an opening that may often transpose to other lines. It is rarely played by masters and tournament players, as the c-pawn is blocked, disallowing it from contesting the d5-pawn. Nonetheless, this line is considered sound and leads to closed positions involving much slow, strategic maneuvering.

Black can also reasonably play 2...e6 (which likely leads to the aforementioned lines), 2...c6 (likely transposing to the Caro–Kann after 3.e4), 2...g6, 2...Bf5, or even 2...f5!? (the Dutch Variation), 2...c5!? (the Irish Gambit, which is a fairly unexplored option), or the unclear 2...e5!? (the Shaviliuk Gambit).

notes.text: The Albin gambit: your pawn hits d4, and after dxe5 d4 you get a strong central wedge.
notes.original:
The Albin Countergambit is an uncommon defense to the Queen's Gambit. Although it is rarely played by masters, it seems to be better than its reputation.

The usual continuation is 3.dxe5 d4, where in exchange for the gambit pawn Black has a central wedge at d4 and gets some chances for an attack. Often White will try to return the pawn at an appropriate moment in order to gain a positional advantage.

The Black pawn at d4 is stronger than it may appear. The careless move 4.e3? can lead to the Lasker Trap (see diagram below). After 4...Bb4+ 5.Bd2 dxe3!! 6.Bxb4?? is a blunder — 6...exf2+! 7.Ke2 fxg1=N+!! and Black's position is superior. The Lasker Trap is notable because it is rare to see an underpromotion as early as move 7.

Instead the game usually continues 4.Nf3 Nc6 (4...c5 allows 5.e3 because Black no longer has the bishop check) and now White's primary options are 5.a3, 5.Nbd2, and 5.g3. Perhaps White's surest try for an advantage is to fianchetto his king bishop with 5.g3 followed by Bg2 and Nbd2.Black will often castle queenside. A typical continuation is 5.g3 Be6 6.Nbd2 Qd7 7.Bg2 O-O-O 8.O-O Bh3.

In the Spassky Variation, White plays 4.e4 to take advantage of the fact that an en passant capture must be made immediately after the enemy pawn moves. Now after 4...Bb4+ 5.Bd2 the en passant capture ...dxe3 is no longer available for Black because of the intervening moves.

notes.text: Your pawn on d4 takes the c3 square away from White.
notes.original: Black takes the c3 square from white.

notes.text: White develops calmly and stays out of any trouble.
notes.original: White stays out of any trouble.

notes.text: You are already better here, and a trap many players fall into is coming.
notes.original: Black's already better. I'll show a trap that many many players have fallen for.

notes.text: Your knight backs up the d4 wedge and eyes White's extra pawn on e5.
White fianchettos its bishop, avoiding tricks and keeping things simple.
notes.original: The Fianchetto Variation. White avoids any tricks from black and keeps things simple.

notes.text: Your bishop attacks the knight that guards e5 and eyes your d4 pawn.
Your knight is rerouting to g6.
notes.original: Rerouting to g6.

notes.text: You develop the bishop because you want to castle queenside.
notes.original: Black wants to castle queenside.

notes.text: Your queen clears the way to castle long and backs a bishop trade on h3.
Your king tucks away and your rook lines up behind the queen to support d4.
White simply keeps developing, bringing its bishop to g2.
notes.original: We just continue developing.

notes.text: White's king is safe and its bishop is fianchettoed, while you wasted time chasing the e5 pawn.
notes.original: White's king is safe and we have a fianchetto'd LSB. Meanwhile, black for the last moves has just wasted time trying to win the e5 pawn back.

notes.text: White sets a quick trap: taking on c4 looks free, but Qa4 check wins your knight.
notes.original: Setting up a quick trap.

notes.text: The check makes White block, and blocking with the bishop walks into your trap.
Your pawn hits the bishop and f2, so grabbing your bishop runs into a check.
The bishop looks free, but it isn't: your e3 pawn takes on f2 with check.
notes.original: Wow, a free bishop! Sadly, no, white can resign now.

notes.text: The king cannot take your pawn: it would leave White's queen to yours.
Promoting to a knight with check is the only move that wins on the spot.
notes.original: A brilliant move! This is actually the only move that wins on the spot.

notes.text: You take the pawn back, and your queen joins the e-pawn against d4.
Your queen escapes the knight by taking d4, where your e-pawn backs it up.
You take the queen back, and your pawn now hits the knight on c3.
Your knight guards c7, so White's knight can't fork your king and rook there.
Your bishop comes out with check, so White must block or move its king.
Trading bishops with check pulls White's king to d2, so it can't castle.
Your pawn hits the undefended knight on d4 and drives it from the centre.
Your knight comes out eyeing e4, and your king is now free to castle.
Your knight comes out eyeing e4, and your king is now free to castle.
Your pawn gives c5 a second defender and opens b7 for your bishop.
You swap off your attacked e-pawn, and White's recapture opens the e-file.
Your knight backs up the d5 pawn, ready to recapture there instead of your queen.
Grabbing on c4 falls for a trap: Qa4 check wins your knight.
notes.original: A nice trap you'll probably get if your opponent's not really paying attention.

notes.text: White sacrifices a pawn for a ton of compensation.
notes.original: Sacrificing a pawn, for a ton of compensation!

notes.text: White is a pawn down, but its pieces are active and the d, e and f files are open.
notes.original: White's pieces are all well placed, ready to attack the black king. White may be down a pawn, but has the open d,e, and f files for attack.

notes.text: White has a clear advantage here, about two and a half pawns.
notes.original: White has a +2.6 advantage.

notes.text: White has won your knight and is simply a piece up.
notes.original: White's simply up a piece.

notes.text: The retreat to c1 looks awkward, but the bishop is best placed there.
notes.original: It may seem awkward to do this, but the bishop is best placed here.

notes.text: White's knight on d2 keeps the c4 pawn protected.
notes.original: Keeping c4 protected.

notes.text: White's king is safe, so it can now start pushing its queenside pawns.
notes.original: White has a 61% winrate. White has a solid kingside, and we can now start launching some pawns at the queenside.

notes.text: Your bishop checks the king and White loses the queen behind it: the Lasker Trap.
notes.original: White loses the lady. This is the Lasker Trap.

notes.text: Mirroring White's moves like this is not a refutation of the London.
notes.original: We've all seen it - your opponent goes for the old "mirror their moves until they make a mistake" trick when they don't know your opening. No matter their reason, this is not a refutation of the London.

notes.text: Whether Bf5 comes before or after Nf6, White answers with c4 straight away.
notes.original: Black can play Bf5 before or after Nf6, but the move order doesn't change your response to it--c4 immediately. Also note c6, which also intends for an early Bf5 (and can be thought of as a little brother to the more potent 2... c5, covered in chapter 4).

notes.text: With your bishop already outside the pawns, e6 backs up d5 and frees your other bishop.
White offers a bishop trade, and swapping is the way to go.
notes.original: Swapping bishops is the way to go here.

notes.text: You swap off White's light bishop, the piece that usually aims at your king.
White has recaptured and simply carries on with the usual London setup.
notes.original: And now we just continue the London setup as per usual.

notes.text: Nf6 is fine here; in Carlsen–Giri Black played c6 instead.
notes.original: In Carlsen - Giri, c6 was played instead here but Nf6 is good too.

notes.text: Your c-pawn challenges White's d4 pawn and gains space on the queenside.
Your knight joins the c-pawn in pressing on d4 while keeping the centre tension.
Even with different opening moves, White still has the b3 and e4 pawn breaks.
notes.original: Different opening moves, still allows for b3 and e4 pawn breaks!

notes.text: Your bishop challenges White's London bishop on f4, offering to trade it off.
You trade off White's London bishop, the key piece of its setup.
You castle before White uses the open h-file; your knight on f6 guards h7.
White now wants b3 to hit your c4 pawn.
notes.original: Now b3 is on the cards.

notes.text: White's e3 is the only good move here.
notes.original: Important to note that this is the only good move here. Observe the alternatives:

notes.text: The early knight move puts White on the back foot: you can reach the good London setup yourself.
notes.original: This unassuming move actually puts white on the back foot, as black can end up in the same very good position we'll be examining for white, but just a tempo down (which doesn't matter that much). This line is why Bf4 comes before Nf3. Without having to waste a tempo on Nf3, the following line offers no danger.

notes.text: Nd2 dodges the bad Nf3 line, but the author finds it very questionable for White.
notes.original: It protects against the bad line that occurs after Nf3 (since the rook can move if the exact same moves are played), but it seems very questionable to me. The main reason for this is that after

notes.text: This is the last moment to develop your bishop to f5, before e6 would shut it in.
notes.original: And this is the latest that black can play Bf5, since e6 would block off the bishop and c5 Bf5 would fail:

notes.text: For concrete reasons, c4 is White's only good response to your bishop move.
notes.original: For very concrete reasons, this is the only good response.

notes.text: Passive setups like Nbd7 and Qc8 don't change much; White keeps a rock-solid advantage.
notes.original: Black can also play Nbd7 and then Qc8 after Qb3, but this is very passive and it's unlikely that he will. Either way you'll have a rock-solid advantage.

notes.text: Your bishop on d6 faces White's London bishop and wants to trade it off.
notes.original: Black continues his ambition--creating his own London bishop and then trying to get rid of yours!

notes.text: Your bishop pins the c3 knight to the king, which limits White's Qb3; it is effective but rare.
notes.original: Yet another ambitious bishop move, creating an annoying pin and limiting the effectiveness of Qb3. A very effective, but rare, line.

notes.text: Qb6 is the move you'll almost always see here; the alternatives are very rare.
notes.original: The only move that you're at all likely to see. In fact, I've never seen anybody play either of the two (relatively) viable alternatives OTB, and almost never online. This is despite this line being pretty popular below master level for whatever reason. Still, it's worth taking a super quick look at the alternatives.

notes.text: Qc8 is a passive defence; White plans to take on d5, then develop with Be2, Rc1 and Nf3.
notes.original: The passive way to defend the pawn. Note that Qe7 would leave black unable to develop normally with Nbd7. In this line, like in the Qb6 line, black is passive, lacking any real winning chances. You should play cxd5 and then develop from here with Be2, Rc1, Nf3, and you can look for an attack on either side of the board.

notes.text: Defending b7 with b6 is the engine way, but it is rare and weakening.
notes.original: The engine way to defend b7. Not a fun move to play, and people don't. I've never seen anyone play this, but it is technically viable, despite being weakening.

notes.text: This is the favorite line: Black has no winning chances and White dominates.
notes.original: Now, after that obnoxious amount of nonsense about other lines and proper move order and whatnot, we finally arrive at our destination. This is my single favorite line in the entirety of the London System. This is for a couple reasons. For one, black has no winning chances, as you'll see. The resulting position will be all white, and it'll be a question of if black can hold on (perhaps even create a fortress). I've never lost a game in this line OTB, and I've seen it a lot (the fact that I see it a lot is the other reason). I'm not even sure I've ever drawn. Many of my wins don't even last 20 moves. As you'll see, white is absolutely dominating.

notes.text: Trading queens is forced: your queen has no retreat square that still protects the b7 pawn.
notes.original: Forced. Black has nowhere to retreat to hold the b7 pawn.

notes.text: White threatens to take your b8 knight with the bishop, then your a7 pawn; just develop the knight.
notes.original: Note that you're threatening Bxb8 and Rxa7 if black doesn't move his knight or play a6 (but there's no reason for him to play a6 now instead of developing)

notes.text: White plays h3 to give the London bishop the h2 square against Nh5, avoiding complications.
notes.original: Not the "best" line, but an easier alternative because it avoids the complications after Nh5. Your London bishop is very important in this position. As such, it makes sense to immediately give it the h2 square against Nh5. In this line, you'll play similarly, with b4 following as well as Nf3, but you're unlikely to be able to get b5 off cleanly, as black will castle and play a6. Then you'll want Nd2-b3-a5, as will be discussed later. You also might go for g4 soon.

notes.text: Your Nh5 leads to complications, but they are good complications for White.
notes.original: Complications results from this, but they're good complications.

notes.text: If you play Nh5, White answers with h3 and keeps the same pressure.
notes.original: If Nh5, you play the exact same thing as in the other line (Bc7 to e5 after being attacked), except instead of Be2 to exploit black's vulnerable pieces, you play h3. It still works.

notes.text: White's f3 prepares g4 and h4, and the knight trip e2, c1, b3 and a5.
notes.original: An interesting option for white. This is followed by g4 and the ideas of b5, Nge2-c1-b3-a5, and h4. I think that Nf3 is easier and simpler, but this is great too.

notes.text: Your a6 only stops b5 if you get castled first; here White can still play b5.
notes.original: I include this line because it gives me a chance to showcase the other winning idea (the main winning idea is just b5), which is relevant if you play a slower move order (like h3, or even just not playing b4 as quickly). In these cases, black will be able to castle and then play a6, stopping b5. Note that here it doesn't stop b5 and you can just play it, transposing into the O-O line.

notes.text: White threatens to take on c6 and win your pawn with Ba6 and Bb7; taking on b5 opens your queenside.
notes.original: Already black is in a pinch. If he doesn't do anything, white can play bxc6 bxc6 Ba6, followed by Bb7, winning the pawn and the game. But if he takes his queenside is blown open.

notes.text: This bishop ties down your f6 knight and threatens c6, which would win at least a pawn.
notes.original: An annoying move. This immobilizes his f6 knight, which otherwise would've been his only useful piece after Ne4. It also immediately threatens c6, which would win at least a pawn if black just played a "normal" move like h6. Black can play a6 to kick it out, but not without a cost.

notes.text: Your rook stops White's c6 push by watching the c-file.
notes.original: Preventing c6.

notes.text: White threatens to take your d7 knight, then your e7 bishop.
notes.original: Threatening Bxd7 Nxd7 Bxe7

notes.text: White's knight goes after your f5 bishop, your only active piece.
notes.original: To get rid of black's only active piece.

notes.text: Other retreats run into trouble: e4 meets f3, and c2 meets king d2, bishop b3 and rook a3.
notes.original: If Be4 f3, and if Bc2 Kd2 Bb3 Ra3

notes.text: Pushing the h-pawn looks tempting, but it loses.
notes.original: Black might be tempted to play this, but it loses

notes.text: Your pieces stay tangled with no play, and White can push on either wing.
notes.original: Black has absolutely nothing. He still can't untangle his pieces, and white can calmly castle (or put his king on e2) and start pushing his b pawn to devastating effect. He could also do the same with his h pawn. The best part is that black has no play whatsoever. This position is winning. The common thread with all these positions we've looked at in this line is that black has very, very little to do. His rooks are forever trapped in passivity, and his minor pieces will forever be worse than their white counterparts. White has black in a stranglehold and can exploit black's lack of play and general entanglement on either the kingside or the queenside. Overall, this line is a disaster for black. Despite this, it's one of the more common lines to see all the way up to close to expert level. After all, if you don't know how to play against Bf5, black is very likely to equalize. If you know to play c4 and force the queen exchange, though, it goes from a frustrating opening to play against to the most fun one to play against. For much of my time playing this line, my knowledge after the queen exchange has been a little fuzzy and unrefined, but I still have consistently destroyed people because I knew to go for b5, and if not that, Nf3-d2-b3-a5. Black isn't going to play optimally enough to test you, so you don't have to know the specifics of all this stuff well. Try to remember those plans and absorb some of the ideas underlying the tactics, as well as some of the secondary stuff like h3 being important and g4 being more or less free. Don't worry too much about the minutiae.

notes.text: You are losing.
White's bishop goes to e2 to hit your potentially vulnerable a6 pawn.
notes.original: Best to move the bishop this way to threaten the potentially vulnerable a6 pawn.

notes.text: Your rook stops any c6 ideas by watching the c-file.
notes.original: Stopping any potential ideas of c6.

notes.text: White castles first; playing h3 here would be wrong.
notes.original: Note that h3 is wrong

notes.text: Your knight can trade off White's strong London bishop, but much of the damage is already done.
notes.original: Black can get rid of your very powerful London bishop, but much of the damage is already done.

notes.text: White plans to double rooks on the a-file and push b5, winning a pawn and freeing the c-pawn.
notes.original: Followed by doubling up on the a-file and b5, which should win at least a pawn, and then the c6 pawn will be free to run. Black has nothing to counter this plan, so we can conclude this here.

notes.text: White follows with b4 and still keeps a crushing grip on you.
notes.original: Followed by b4, etc. White is still crushing.

notes.text: Now you are in control: White's bishop on a6 is pinned to its rook on a1.
notes.original: All of a sudden, black is in control. The bishop is pinned to the a1 rook.

notes.text: You threaten Bd3, so White's c5 pawn must fall and White's edge disappears.
notes.original: And black is threatening Bd3, so the pawn must fall, and with it, white's advantage.

notes.text: This bishop jump to a6 is how White wins most games in this line.
notes.original: Most of the games I've won in this line have been because of bxc6 bxc6 Ba6.

notes.text: White's strongest move here is still b5; h3 is a slower try shown for demonstration.
notes.original: Again, b5 is right here, but this is for demonstration purposes.

notes.text: White signals a dangerous knight trip: from d2 to b3, then on to a5.
notes.original: Signaling a dangerous maneuver: Nf3-d2-b3-a5.

notes.text: Against Na5 you have only two answers: b6 drops the a6 pawn, and b5 leaves a6 hopelessly weak.
notes.original: Black has only two options against Na5 here, since b6 would drop a6 and b5 would weaken the a6 pawn beyond the point of saving.

notes.text: A rook on a7 to guard the pawn is unappealing, but answering Na5 with b6 can look scary too.
notes.original: Who would want to put their rook on a7 to defend the pawn? Probably no one, but playing b6 against Na5 might seem scary to some as well.

notes.text: Your knight move ignores Na5 and leaves you defending a6 in the most passive way, with Ra7.
notes.original: Leaving himself to defend the pawn in the most passive way imaginable.

notes.text: White waits patiently: you can't play b6 unless White plays Na5, and otherwise you lack any play.
notes.original: Patience. Black can't play b6 unless you play Na5, and without that he's lacking any play.

notes.text: Your knight check is hard to avoid, but it actually loses a pawn.
notes.original: What else could black even possibly do? It's very hard to come up with anything else, but this actually loses a pawn. If black doesn't play this, he'll have to maybe push g5 and then shuffle his pieces around, waiting for you to kill him. Might as well just go for this.

notes.text: White is a pawn up and you are passive; winning will be a slow but comfortable grind for White.
notes.original: White's now up a pawn. Black once again is pretty passive, but the process of winning will remain a bit of slog. A comfortable slog, though.

notes.text: White's knight sacrifice on b7 is a thematic idea in this line.
notes.original: A thematic sac in this line.

notes.text: White's rook will win your c6 pawn with Rc8, and the connected passed pawns will be unstoppable.
notes.original: The c6 pawn will fall to Rc8, and the connected passers will be unstoppable.

notes.text: Taking on d7 shows how strong White's bishops are in this line.
notes.original: A demonstration of the strength of white's bishop pair.

notes.text: Your pawn hits the knight on a5; if White backs off, you follow with a5.
notes.original: The idea, then a5 if white backs off.

notes.text: Ra7 is forced and your rook is shut out, so White will play on the kingside.
notes.original: Forced. This position looks unbelievably bleak for black, but it isn't lost yet. I've ended up in this position before and I was shocked at how resilient black's defenses actually can be (although I did win, so take that with a grain of salt). In fact, you should be trying to create play on the kingside, since the queenside is pretty solid for now and black's a7 rook is locked out of the game.

notes.text: White's f3 gives you the chance to connect your rooks.
notes.original: You want to connect your rooks, and this gives you the chance to.

notes.text: White's bishop goes to c7 so your e5 can't block it; otherwise Bb6 would be threatened.
notes.original: Since black wants e5, it's best to keep your bishop from being blocked by it. It also would threaten Bb6 if black didn't play e5, but he won't.

notes.text: Your bishop retreats to d8 because you hardly have a choice against White's Bb6 idea.
notes.original: Black hardly has a choice, since he has to deal with Bb6.

notes.text: Your a7 rook is stuck until you protect c6 and play b6, so White is effectively an exchange up.
notes.original: I'm not going to take any more of your time showing this long, drawn out line, so here's the rundown of what's important: Black's rook is stuck on a7 until he protects c6 and plays b6, which will create horrible weaknesses and almost definitely lose at least the a6 pawn (you can just take and drop the knight back). Because black's rook is stuck over there, you're effectively playing an exchange up. On top of this, black continues to have no play, while you have plenty of prospects. This should be winning, but you'd have to be a little careful, because it's not going to be super easy.

notes.text: White's bishop on e5 is very strong, and trying to chase it away will backfire on you.
notes.original: Black just wanted to get rid of your powerful bishop, but right about now he's probably realizing that it's a fool's errand.

notes.text: Your f6 pawn takes away the last escape square of your own knight on h5.
notes.original: Black still wants to get rid of the bishop, but this removes the knight's only escape square.

notes.text: Your a6 is probably the best try here, though it means backing off.
notes.original: Probably best, but who'd back off now?

notes.text: White threatens to win your a7 pawn, and Be2 would also trap your knight.
notes.original: And this is like 11... Nxe5, but slightly little less bad (not saying much). White is threatening both Rxa7, winning a pawn, and Be2, winning a piece.

notes.text: You are a pawn down with a shattered position, and White is winning.
notes.original: Black's down a pawn and his entire position is in shambles. White is winning.

notes.text: Your a7 pawn hangs, and defending it with a6 lets Be2 win a piece.
notes.original: There are many problems for black now. One is that a7 is hanging. If he plays a6 to defend it, Be2 will win a piece. If he saves his knight/bishop with g5, a7 falls, and black loses anyway.

notes.text: White's bishop attacks your trapped knight on h5 and threatens a fork.
notes.original: Attacking the trapped knight and threatening a fork.

notes.text: You are losing.
You are losing.
You wasted time chasing the bishop, and your position has only got worse.
notes.original: Black has totally wasted his time and only made things worse.

notes.text: Taking back with the knight is possible, but it gives up your claim to the center.
notes.original: is also a possibility, but it's unlikely black will want to give up his claim to the center

notes.text: White threatens to jump the knight to b5.
notes.original: Threatening Nb5

notes.text: Your a5 is an active way to meet the Nb5 threat.
notes.original: Preventing Nb5 actively

notes.text: The obvious way to stop Nb5, but more passive than a5; both weaken your dark squares.
notes.original: the obvious way to address the threat, but it's more passive than the sharp a5 (note that both create potentially dangerous dark-square weakness on the queenside). Play this position in the same way you'd play against a5.

notes.text: White's h3 prepares g4 and gives the London bishop a retreat square on h2.
notes.original: h3 is very important in these lines to prepare g4 and give your London bishop a square to retreat to

notes.text: White's knight jump is bad: you hit the queen with a4, then Bb4 checks.
notes.original: is bad because of

notes.text: White's g4 hits your bishop, and you lack the activity to punish this aggression.
notes.original: Thematic in these lines. Black can't punish this aggression because of his lack of activity.

notes.text: Bg6 is a mistake, because White answers with h4.
notes.original: Is bad because of

notes.text: Don't take on g4; White's h5 threatens to win your bishop.
notes.original: black can't take on g4. If knight takes then Nxd5, since c6 is pinned, and if Qxg4 then Qxb7. Either way white would be much better. White threatens h5 immediately, winning the bishop (since Be4 f3 doesn't save it).

notes.text: White's pieces are very active here.
notes.original: So much activity!

notes.text: You had to block with Nbd7, because moving the queen would lose your b7 pawn.
notes.original: Black has no choice--he can't get his queen away from the discovery with because b7 will fall, so he has to block.

notes.text: White wins a pawn on d5 after a quick kingside attack, and Qc8 leaves you passive.
notes.original: Winning a pawn and probably the game. Note how quickly that kingside attack developed. Black is passive and really struggles to defend against all of the threats. In general, Qc8 just leaves black in a tough position to try to defend, with slim to no winning chances. Nobody wants to play it.

notes.text: Your bishop checks the king and forces White to react.
The position is sharp, but you are clearly better.
notes.original: Sharp, but definitively better for black.

notes.text: White keeps a strong center and better activity; if you trade knights, the b-pawn retakes.
notes.original: And you'll enjoy a strong center and better activity. If black eventually exchanges knights, bxc3 will likely be better, opening even more paths to controlling the center whether it be protecting d4 to prepare an e4 push or simply pushing c4.

notes.text: White opens the c-file to attack your weakened c6 pawn.
notes.original: clearing the c-file such that the weakened c-pawn can be attacked

notes.text: White's knight development is also fine here, even though your b6 weakened the queenside.
notes.original: Is also fine

notes.text: You recapture with the pawn; taking with the knight leads to similar play.
notes.original: Recapture if instead Nxd5, and play will continue similarly.

notes.text: White develops and keeps the bishop on f4, so a trade there strengthens White's grip on e5.
notes.original: What you should be playing if you end up here. Same idea as in the main line with Bd6 without c5--leave your bishop on f4 so that if he takes, you strengthen your hold on e5. Controlling e5 is even more important in this position, since it attacks the weakened pawn on c6.

notes.text: Ne5 is White's best but very complicated line, so stay alert here.
notes.original: This line is too complicated to reasonably play given the obscurity of b6 to begin with, but it is optimal. Black can't afford to fall asleep at the wheel here.

notes.text: Your knight can't go to d7, because White's bishop would take your d6 bishop; expect a trade.
notes.original: Black can't play Nd7 because the d6 bishop would fall, and obviously it would hang on a6, so he is very likely to exchange bishops now.

notes.text: Your knight move allows a tactic: White's knight takes on c6, followed by Bb5.
notes.original: It takes sharp tactical insight to take advantage of this, but Nxc6 Bb5 is the idea. If black plays something more normal like castling, you can develop normally with Be2, etc.

notes.text: White's g4 pawn attacks both your bishop on f5 and your knight on h5.
notes.original: Intermediate move

notes.text: Resolving the tension by taking on e5 also runs into problems for you.
notes.original: The other way to resolve this also runs into problems

notes.text: White takes the weak c6 pawn; this tactic is very unlikely, so don't memorize it.
notes.original: And finally, the point. You shouldn't be trying to memorize this tactical sequence, by the way. It's so absurdly unlikely that you ever end up in the position that initiates it, and I only really cover it for my own sake and because it shows how the c6 weakness is actually relevant (and how g4 can sometimes punish Nh5 when the bishop is on f5).

notes.text: White's queen attacks your h5 knight, and White ends up two pawns ahead.
notes.original: This attacks the h5 knight, giving you a tempo to play d5, getting your piece back and leaving you up two pawns. There's no way you're seeing all of this after 9... Nh5 unless you're absolutely insane--you would have to remember all this stuff. Ne5 is the optimal line, but maybe it'd be best to avoid it.

notes.text: White's center is overwhelming, and e4 will soon remove what holds your position together.
notes.original: And white has way, way more than enough compensation for the pawn. White's center is overwhelming (and can be easily fortified with f4) and e4 will come soon, obliterating the tiny shred of protection holding black's position together.

notes.text: White will win the pawn back on g7 and keep a strong initiative.
notes.original: The pawn will quickly be regained (on g7) and white will have a very strong initiative

notes.text: White can also jump to e5, though the author finds taking on d5 easier to play.
notes.original: etc. I think cxd5 is easier to play.

notes.text: White will follow with Bb5+, Nf3 and b4, keeping a slight, drawish edge.
notes.original: Followed by Bb5+, Nf3, b4, etc. Drawish but definitely better for white, who will be in the driver's seat even if he doesn't have that much.

notes.text: White gets a solid center, and your queenside pawns look a little vulnerable; this line is rare.
notes.original: Or Qxc3, but I prefer to not give black a tempo for Ne4. White has a solid center with backup at c3 (which may eventually come into play after a trade and c4), and black's queenside pawns are looking a little vulnerable.. Complications now arise after both Na5 Qb4 and O-O Qxb7, but this line is rare enough that spending time exploring them is unnecessary.

notes.text: White's a3 stops your bishop from coming to b4 with an annoying pin.
notes.original: To prevent the annoying Bb4

notes.text: Note the limitations of having put your knight on c6 in this line.
notes.original: Note the limitations of putting the knight on c6:

notes.text: You could avoid the trade with dxc4, but that gives up your center and leaves White solidly better.
notes.original: He could also play dxc4 to prevent this exchange, but that would give up his claim to the center and leave you solidly better after Bxc4.

notes.text: White has the better center and more activity, so watch the queenside, especially the c-file.
notes.original: With a better center and more activity. In some ways this will play out like a typical London, but you'll want to pay special attention to the queenside (and especially the c-file)

notes.text: White wins a pawn on c5, and you can't get it back.
notes.original: And black can't get the pawn back

notes.text: White's b4 holds on to the extra pawn on c5.
notes.original: and if

notes.text: Your a5 pawn attacks b4 to try to break down White's pawn chain.
notes.original: to try to break down the pawn chain

notes.text: In this position White's Nf3 is a disastrous move.
notes.original: is disastrous

notes.text: You have a little compensation, but the pawn isn't coming back; expect White's bishop to go to b5.
notes.original: While black does have a little compensation, the pawn isn't coming back. Look for Bb5 and maybe Nd4/e5

notes.text: Qc2 doesn't work for White in this move order, as your reply shows.
notes.original: Note that this doesn't work in this move order because

notes.text: In this move order your Bf5 loses to White's queen taking it.
notes.original: loses to

notes.text: After this queen trade, Black gets at least a slight edge by force against an early Nf3.
notes.original: We'll observe this position in more depth (but a tempo up, with white being the one who played c4-c5) later to show why this is really bad for the side being forced into this queen exchange. For now, just understand that if you play Nf3 on move 3 against d5 Nf6, black can take at least a slight advantage by force if you stay within the London.

notes.text: Your bishop move leaves you more than equal in this line.
notes.original: And black has more than equalized, since

notes.text: Your queen takes b2 and now attacks the rook on a1, which White loses.
notes.original: loses the rook

notes.text: Your Nf6 is more effective than White's Nd2, so White's extra tempo is illusory.
notes.original: c4 is much less effective. On c3, the knight pressures d5 and forces black to spend moves protecting it, allowing us to execute our plan of Qb3 Qb6 c5. It's also notable that now e3 Bd3 isn't possible for you, which is pretty unfortunate. While you would still be a tempo up in this position, black's Nf6 is more effective than your Nd2, so this advantage is illusory. Consider this position roughly equal.

notes.text: You threaten Qb6, hitting b2 and d5, so White must give up the b2 pawn.
notes.original: This line is still a problem, albeit for a different reason than after Nf3. Black is threatening Qb6, which will attack both b2 and d5. You won't have enough defenders on either, so you'll have to sac the b2 pawn for unclear compensation. The engine will spit out a roughly even evaluation for doing so, but you'd have to be very prepared to find compensation.

notes.text: Taking on b2 leaves White in a hard-to-play, suboptimal position, even if the engine says level.
notes.original: And this looks even worse to me than the other line. In both cases, the engine spits out 0.0, so these lines are playable, but they're very hard to play and suboptimal. Avoid them unless you really, really like these positions for some reason.

notes.text: White has no clear way to punish you for grabbing the b2 pawn.
notes.original: It's very unclear how you're ever going to punish black for grabbing this pawn, initiative be damned.

notes.text: Your e-pawn holds d5 against the c4 pawn, so you keep your centre.
Your c-pawn adds another guard to d5, now hit by White's pawn and knight.
Your queen shields the b7 pawn from White's queen and offers a trade.
This pawn push eventually transposes into the main Bf5 line.
notes.original: And this eventually transposes into the main Bf5 line

notes.text: White plans e3 and Bxc4 to win the pawn back with a comfortable position.
notes.original: Followed by e3 and Bxc4 with a comfortable position

notes.text: After White plays c4 this transposes into the usual lines.
notes.original: Will transpose after c4, etc.

notes.text: White's b3 is almost never right in the London, but against this setup it is best.
notes.original: Please make careful note of the fact that b3 is almost never correct in the London. If your opponent were to play c5 and then Qb6, this would just be wrong. Here, though, it is best.

notes.text: Bd3 against an early Bf5 usually means something went wrong, but here it is fine for White.
notes.original: Note that this line plays very differently than other lines. Typically if you're playing Bd3 against an early Bf5 something has gone wrong, but not here.

notes.text: White has a dominant position: play Nh5 and b5 starts a strong queenside attack; otherwise h3 comes.
notes.original: With a pretty dominant position, similar to the ones you get after the main Bf5 line but with the queens on. If black doesn't play Nh5 you'll want to play h3 here, and if he does you'll play b5 immediately and have a potent queenside attack.

notes.text: White is solidly, slightly better and can develop with Nf3, castling, c4 and Nc3.
notes.original: With a solid, slightly better position. You can continue with Nf3 (or Ne2) O-O c4 Nc3 and enjoy a position that would be very hard to lose.

notes.text: You have several ways to develop, but this knight move is the most common because it is flexible.
notes.original: Black can develop a number of ways, though 2...Nf6 is most common due to its flexibility.

notes.text: Your knight move can transpose to the Nimzowitsch Defence after White plays e4.
notes.original: 2...Nc6 transposes to the Nimzowitsch Defence after 3.e4, normally reached by 1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3.

notes.text: White's main tries now are Bf4, the Jobava London, and Bg5, the Richter-Veresov Attack.
notes.original: The main lines after this are the 2...Nf6 3.Bf4, the Jobava London System, and 2...Nf6 3.Bg5, the Richter–Veresov Attack (which transposes into the French Defense after 3...e6 or remains in independent lines after 3...Nbd7).
